Simulacra is a brilliant horror missing phone game. It is quite similar to a normal/another lost phone, but with a higher budget and fantasy style story.

I really like the game i did many live streams of the game and i really recammend this game.

The thing i did not like about this game is all the jump scares i got scared many times.

Overall, I do like the concept behind Simulacra, it gave me a lot of flashbacks to a game called Orwell which also had a very voyeristic/technological vibe and left me wanting to explore more and learn more about the people I was encountering.

However, I have one single criticism of this game based on my experience so far that I think has somewhat soured my opinion of what otherwise seems to be a great horror title with a novel concept, that being the jump scares.

They're completely unessercary and feel rather out of place, the situation the game presents you with is already creepy and uncomfortable enough on it's own without needing to throw up distorted pictures with loud bursts of white noise, it didn't draw me deeper into the experience, it actually yanked me firmly out of it and discouraged me from further exploring the various areas of the phone and probing for more details and information (seeing as I'm not particularly fond of jump scares and random exploration seems like a good way to stumble upon them).

I'd say if someone was going to make another game in this style, have confidence that your concept is creepy enough to draw people in, it'd make a nice change to see more horror titles content to let their horror have a slow, deep burn rather than a quick, short lived flash.

I like the new digital horror like Doki Doki and Simulacra. You wake up, find a phone, and get a call on it that people are looking for the owner
 You get roped into a world of this girl where people are scared for her, accusing you, and you have to be on your toes to defend yourself and also make sure you don't give the wrong information to the wrong people.

Sure it's over the top on the scenario but that's the game. That's the entertainment. I'm glad I bought this and played it.

After playing Sara is Missing and hearing about Simulacra through that purveyor of all things horror-related, Night Mind, I decided to check it out.  I was pleasantly surprised.  The story is much more developed compared to SiM, and I enjoyed exploring Anna's phone.  The concept of the game was much more interesting than SiM, though I feel like it could still be better developed and hope the devs continue with this idea.  While the text speak used by the main "players" of the game was perfectly realistic, I felt that the primary antagonist of the game [spoiler]Simulacra[/spoiler] would not have the spelling errors I encountered in that character's texting.  For instance, the character used "lead" instead of "led" and "it's" when "its" was intended.  I know, I know, others might not have noticed or been affected by this, but I felt that the character would not have made those errors.

Overall, the characters were better developed than SiM, definitely.  Anna was three-dimensional, and so were the characters we encountered.  Omitting Iris [spoiler]though of course allusions can be found in the website, thanks to the phone number and Morse Code[/spoiler], was a good decision.  I don't know if the plan is for DLC or sequels, but I look forward to a continuation of the Simulacra and/or Iris story-line, in this world where technology has a mind of its own.

For the devs:
[list]
[*]The ambiance is brilliant.  I love the room behind the phone, the lights flickering and the sounds around me.  It definitely creates an aura of suspense.
[*]As far as jump scares, I agree with Night Mind, unnecessary, kind of lame, and ineffective.
[*]What did solving the puzzles accomplish?  I mean, I don't know if I had to unscramble the photos and texts to progress, I just always do it to get it out of the way, but they don't, in the story, progress anything, really, [spoiler]until the Spark conversation with James[/spoiler].  Also they were really easy.  When you present me with a four-word scramble...come on.
[*]Where is this supposed to take place?  The accents were peculiar.  It seemed like you were aiming for American, but you were using British spellings, i.e. favourite.  Is it meant to take place in Canada?
[*]I did love the multiple endings, and felt much more invested in them than I did in SiM.  In particular, [spoiler]I just achieved the happy ending, and afterward, stared at the screen and said, "Did I just get possessed?  I think I just got possessed."[/spoiler]
[*][spoiler]Even if you're interviewing through text (for reasons?), why would you consider hiring a person to be a copywriter who makes that many spelling and grammatical errors?  I kept looking at my response options, and they were painful.  Yes, I understand you're not really applying and just trying to get information about James, but still.[/spoiler]
[/list]
All that being said, I do hope you continue and would love to play any other games set in this world.  If you appreciate nothing else from my review, let it be: less is more.  Subtle horror is better than overt horror.  The idea that somebody might be in the room with you, where you're holding that phone, or the idea that you might lower the phone and see, I don't know, a floating disembodied head, was so much more effective than momentary flashes of the screen turning into something scary.  And if [spoiler]the final image had been the player lowering the screen and something vague and shadowy, or even a representation of the Simulacra, being there, and then moving toward the screen if you simply must jump scare, it would have been better than the shift in Anna's picture.[/spoiler]  It's the suspense that gets you, not the actual scare.  You don't have the suspense before the jump scares on the phone, just an image shift.

Nevertheless, public who have reached this far (or TLDR), I do recommend this game.  It isn't a long game, but I've spent...7 hours in it so far?  And intend to spend more unlocking achievements.

I'm a huge fan of this kind of voyeuristic mystery genre, and this is one of the best I've come across. 
The mixing of platforms; text, audio and FMV, creates a very realistic and immersive phone to explore. The level of detail inside the phone apps is also unparallelled. You can explore people's profiles on the dating app and strike up a conversation with someone inconsequential, you can read comments on posts on the social media app, you can read spam emails. So much detail was put into building the world.
The characters (while the voice and visual acting can be a little hokey) each have their own distinct personalities through texts and messages, the writing there is spot on, plus you can interact with them in so many different ways it feels like your voice really matters to the plot.   
I was put off this game initially because I'm a huge wimp and not a big horror fan, but the scares never made me want to stop playing, and it was really worth it.
11/10 I can't wait for the next game from these guys.

This review may contain light spoilers. The TL;DR is that I would recommend it, it's about 3 hours of gameplay, but is quite hand-holdy in parts. Don't go into this expecting a cerebral game where you need to figure everything out for yourself. Also, don't expect the choices the game forces you into making to make any sense, either.

I quite liked it. It's definitely an improvement from the last game, but there are a few things I noticed.
For instance, there's a few grammar and spelling mistakes in the phone's interface through the game, and most notably the 'BUSTED' chatroom, after it's just 2 people left in it, turns into 'BUSTED' is typing, as if the contact name was called 'BUSTED' and this wasn't actually a chatroom.

The knocking, gasps/breathing 'outside' the phone (This game could also be titled "Millennials don't answer the door simulator 2017") were also unneeded. It wasn't that scary and took away from the game, if you're going I was expecting a jump-scare, or some kind of mechanic where I would need to move around my house to avoid various hostile entities from 'getting me' while I solved the phone mystery. 

It was also a bit too linear and railroady for my tastes. The auto-suggestion mechanic needs a lot more work because I felt like I was constantly being railroaded in the dialogue sections down a path that there's no way I (as a person) would have done or said. I wasn't a fan of the two 'supposed-to-lose' parts, either - I spent a good half an hour on one, hunting around and going into every app and going through every bit of information I had so far trying to get more information. 

The story felt very one-track also. If you compared this game to a visual novel, which is pretty much what this game is, a standard VN player would be very dissapointed with the lack of branching paths, different dialogues, and small amount of endings.

I really want to emphasize that the 'free-roam' hunting for information was the best part of this game, and the dialogue elements forcefeeding you stuff you figured out 10 messages ago was the absolute worst. If the devs want to keep on making games like these, the dialog absolutely needs more work. Additionally it seems like the developers really wanted to characterize these people but in the process of haphazardly sprinkling photographs in there were serious inconsistences. Players are going to be combing through this stuff trying to find precious information and the last thing they need is to be misled due to a mistake.

Overall, though, I recommend a buy if this is the sort of game you like. This is a vast improvement upon the last game and I look forward to this studio's next game.

Simulacra is a simulated mobile phone method of delivering a horror game. It is based on the disappearance of a young woman named Anna, and the protagonist (you) has discovered her phone on their doorstep. From there, you delve into the secrets of her phone to find all the information you can, and try to locate--and subsequently save--Anna.

From a mechanical perspective, the game is pretty solid. There's no skeleton or standard out there for "Phone application based horror", making Simulacra a rather noteworthy pioneer and sequel to the developer's predecessor. Applications are sound, mimicking their real-life counterparts exceptionally well. The interface is smooth, and the methods for accessing the different pools of data prove acceptable. My only real complaint is, while the "data restoration" mechanic was easy enough to use, it felt ultimately meaningless and proved only to be a minor time sink. It was an interesting concept, but executed poorly. Perhaps, in later editions, the method for restoring and recovering data might make a more central point in the story.

However, in a game like this, the story is what really holds the fiber and and strength of a game. Hoo boy, does Simulacra tell you a story. The deeper you delve, the closer you get, the more stressful the game will become. Information will consistently surprise the player, and force them to make intensely difficult decisions. While they do have some effect on the ending of the game, the limitation to four significant endings does, to say the least, cause some level of dissonance between decision making and results.

Overall, for five dollars, it was a surprisingly binge-worthy experience.

At the time of its release, I was kind of obsessed with Sara is Missing. The style was fresh and new, and what a great idea! Finding a missing person through their phone is already such an interesting mystery, a look at how much of our lives are stored in this technology with a personal touch. However, in the end, I had too many questions that went unanswered, and ultimately felt unsatisfied.

SIMULACRA, on the other hand, has so far fixed all of these issues. For clarity sake, I have only achieved two endings at this time, and have more to go. For the same reason, and to give my respect to the developers, I will say I found this game through NightMind's video. This was one of the very, very few times I actually paused in the middle of a video to go out and buy the game myself - I will admit however, the low price was a factor in that. I was expecting more, but this game was more than worth my money.

There are a few silly little mistakes - Some of which add a level of realism and are undoubtedly intentional, like the varying type styles and occasional grammar errors and misspells... And some which are just a little funny, but in the end, the writing and acting won me over any time I was distracted from the experience. The mystery this time around is far more fun and rewarding to solve, the characters are largely likable (UNLESSANNAWHEREARETHOSEDATAREPORTS) and believable within this context.

The whole theme of using someone's phone to dig through their identity is played with far, FAR more effectively here, and the paranormal aspects (cmon it was obvious) offer some commentary, as well as another interesting character I wanted to explore.

The fact that the game doesn't allow multiple save states to allow choice-scumming for the desired result was at first a bit annoying, I want to see what they would all say if I said this or that, but it does add a certain weight to each choice - If you slip up and don't want to see it through, you have to start over.

There are a few other fun little distractions, if you need a moment of relief from the spooks, such as replying over and over again to the home security bot, replying to other people's tweets with memes, editing Anna's Spark profile the moment you have access to it so that it shows the lyrics to Feel Good Inc. and a picture of her cat, and etc. And even if you do choose to mess around a little it, you can still progress the story whether or not Anna's profile name is now Snart.

While I can't promise poo your pants horror, and the scares will be subjective, it's a fun little game even if you only want to pretend to be another person and gain everyone's trust, or immediately tell everyone you meet that you're not Anna. Or call 911, call her friends, read her texts and emails, waste her phone battery, and etc.

I was pretty impressed with Sarah is Missing when it came out, though it definitely had its flaws. With Simulacra, the developers have clearly built on criticisms of their first game and made for a way more unsettling and entertaining experience. 

The game does rely a bit on jumpscares at times, but not to an excessive or obnoxious degree. Far better is what the game does with subtle ambiant spookiness--things that happen in the background that don't really draw attention to themselves but definitely left me feeling unsettled. 

There are still some things that didn't work for me. The corrupted images and messages were fun, but a little bit too easy, and often didn't really give a satisfying payoff. The voice acting could be kind of hit or miss at times as well, though generally the game was very well acted. But on the whole, it was a great experience, and one of the scariest games I've played this year.

I really don't want to spoil this game for anyone, so I am just going to encourage you to do one thing : just buy SIMULACRA and play it through for yourself. For such a low price I don't think it is a very risky investment, and if you are interested in narration in video games it could be a shame to miss it.

I wouldn't say it's a perfect game, there is still room for improvement, especialy in how the game handles the player doing things out of order. But I would lie if I didn't say that I was glued to my screen from start to finish. Video games are truly different from non-interactive art forms, but sometimes it takes a game like SIMULACRA to remind us of it. To remind us that video games can create experiences that have never been made possible before.

Despite some flaws, this game is a truly unique experience that I would encourage you to experience.  And to maybe leave a review when you are done with it, even if you didn't like it. Because I firmly believe that this is one of those games that can push the medium forward.

I'm surprised. I was expecting something maybe a little hokey or cheesy by the end but what I got was actually a surprisingly effective, creepy tech horror story.

It feels like it wouldn't be out of place as something from the first couple of V/H/S movies. It apes the whole unconventional found footage thing to a tee and despite the occasional spot of grammatical weirdness, it's extremely well made and polished, especially for like five bucks. The acting was reasonably good, the villain was out and out creepy and well done. You can't ask for more, really.

It's about the perfect length for this sort of thing (two to three hours), there's a few puzzles that take some thinking but nothing that's complete and utter nonsense logic and it's replayable and branching with plenty of hidden easter eggs. Kudos to the developers, I'm glad I found out this was a thing.

Simulacra is a fun and notable improvement over Sarah is Missing (SIM).  The game has a more exploration available in terms of the data available on the phone and a few fun offshots to explore.

Unfortunately, the game still suffers from the on-rail feel of SIM.  This stems from what seems to be an idiot protagonist: like  in SIM, many times the options the players are given are all stupid or outright needlessly antagonistic toward allies.  While a protagonist who is too genre-aware would be bad, I would prefer to be able to play a character closer to my headspace than  the often cluelessly bumbling protagonist.

Still, the game has a wonderful presentation and is fun for an inexpensive thriller.  I highly recommend it to anyone looking for a neat way to spend part of an afternoon.
